chapters.title: Feature-Positive Effect
chapters.hook: The visible clue gets a voice; the missing clue has to wait for someone to ask.
chapters.counterintuition: The thing you can see may be less useful than the thing that is absent; name the feature-positive pull, then check what is missing.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one choice based on a visible cue. Write the absent evidence that would change your mind before you act.
chapters.keyTakeaway: The feature-positive effect makes present cues feel stronger than missing evidence. Add an explicit absence check before deciding.

breakdown.fastRead: The call log in the pension app review shows many users asking about a higher default rate. Marjorie wants to raise the default because the calls are visible. The missing cue is quieter: most users never called. The room can see the calls. She writes feature-positive on the log, adds a no-call sample check, and changes the default review only after both groups are visible.
breakdown.deepRead:
Present evidence is easier to use than absent evidence. A mark, symptom, complaint, photo, or phone call gives the mind something to hold. Absence asks for a harder question: what should be here if the claim were true?

The feature-positive effect is this tilt toward what appears. An ambulance review may overfocus on stamped forms and miss the shifts with no forms because nobody completed them. A renovation plan may chase visible cracks and miss rooms with no inspection notes. A watch retailer may treat waitlist names as demand while ignoring customers who left without signing.

Absence needs a search party.

The correction is to ask for the missing cue before the next choice moves. What evidence would be absent if the story were wrong? What group is not represented? What symptom, complaint, form, or data point did not appear? Then design the choice so absence gets a box, not an afterthought.

This matters because visible cues can be genuine and still incomplete. You should not ignore the call, crack, symptom, or form. You should stop it from becoming the whole diagnosis before the missing evidence has been invited in.
breakdown.fullRead:
The stamped form in the ambulance night-shift review shows three delayed handoffs. Cheryl, the operations lead, can see the problem in ink. What she cannot see is just as important: two crews skipped forms entirely during the busiest hour. If the review counts only stamped forms, the cleanest-looking shifts may be the least documented.

The feature-positive effect makes presence feel like proof. A visible cue is easy to count, repeat, and defend. Missing evidence is slippery. It may mean nothing happened. It may mean nobody looked. It may mean the system failed before the record began.

What should be present if your story is true?

Zhao and Pechmann's work on regulatory focus, the feature-positive effect, and message framing used anti-smoking campaigns to study how present and absent features shape response. The broader lesson travels well: people respond strongly to features that are shown, named, or framed, while absence often needs a deliberate prompt to enter judgment.

A vaccine-statistic framing case shows the same force. Beverly sees a site photo of a crowded clinic and wants the message to focus on demand. The absence is harder to see: neighborhoods with low turnout do not show up in the photo. If the campaign follows only the visible crowd, it may speak to the already-engaged and miss the people at risk.

The missing group is data too.

A viral chart fact-check makes the trap plain. Federica sees a blood-test panel that highlights one rising marker. The chart online circles the marker in red and claims a crisis. The absent evidence is the base range, the repeat test, and the people whose marker did not rise. A fact-check that follows the red circle will spread the error faster. A fact-check that asks what is missing can slow it down.

The practical correction is an absence column. Put the visible cue on the left. Put the missing cue on the right. Ask what you would expect to see if the story held, what you would expect to be absent if it were false, and which group is missing from the record. Then decide only after both sides have been named.

The limit is that absence can be ambiguous. No complaint may mean no problem, or no safe way to complain. No symptom may mean health, or a test that cannot detect the disease. The answer is not to worship absence. The answer is to make it visible enough to question.

Before the choice moves forward, give the absent evidence a place to stand. If the visible cue still carries the decision after that, use it. If the choice changes once the missing group appears, the feature was choosing for you.

questions.prompt: In a feature-positive case, a team gives more weight to visible complaints than to the customers who never complained or were never asked, what is the feature-positive effect?
choices: A practice of giving more weight to recent complaints than to historical ones, since recency tracks the team's current operational priorities most directly.
A reflex to address visible problems first, which is a defensible operational principle in customer service contexts across most industries broadly.
A tendency to overweight present cues while underchecking absent evidence.
questions.explanation: The visible complaints may matter, but the missing group needs its own check before the decision follows the visible cue.

questions.prompt: During a feature-positive review, a pension app team wants to change a default rate because callers complain, most users never call. What should the team do before changing the rate?
choices: Change the default rate as proposed, since complaints from any source signal operational issues teams should address quickly under most circumstances.
Compare callers with a sample of users who never called.

questions.explanation: The no-call sample gives absence a voice. Caller complaints alone may overrepresent visible dissatisfaction.

questions.prompt: When feature-positive pressure appears, an ambulance review counts stamped delay forms but ignores crews that filed nothing during peak calls. Which correction fits?
choices: Count missing forms as part of the handoff review.

questions.prompt: After feature-positive risk surfaces, an architect ranks repairs by visible cracks, but several rooms have no inspection notes at all, what should happen first?
choices: Rank repairs by visible crack severity, since visible damage is the strongest signal the architect can use to allocate repair resources fairly across rooms.
Survey building occupants about rooms without notes, since occupant testimony fills the data gap that uninspected rooms would otherwise create for the ranking.
Inspect or flag rooms with no notes before ranking the repair list.
questions.explanation: Blank rooms are absent evidence, not proof of safety. The repair ranking needs to know whether those rooms were actually checked.

questions.prompt: If feature-positive reasoning takes over, a retailer treats a watch waitlist as total demand, but staff report many customers leave when asked to sign up. What is the likely error?
choices: The waitlist is being treated as diagnosis while walkouts are ignored.
The waitlist sign-up process is poorly designed, since well-designed sign-up flows convert most interested customers into committed waitlist participants without dropouts.
The watch model itself has demand-supply mismatch, since strong waitlist demand should not coexist with widespread walkouts under any realistic demand curve.
questions.explanation: The waitlist shows visible demand, but walkouts are missing demand data. The buying plan needs both.

questions.prompt: While feature-positive pressure builds, a vaccine campaign uses crowded clinic photos to frame demand, but low-turnout neighborhoods appear in none of the images, what should the next message include?
choices: More crowded clinic photos, since visible demand signals encourage hesitant individuals to participate in the kind of campaign behavior the team is trying to drive.
Photos from low-turnout neighborhoods that show recently improved turnout, since visible improvement narratives often outperform abstract demographic comparisons in messaging.
Crowded clinics and the low-turnout neighborhoods missing from the images.
questions.explanation: The crowded photo captures presence. The missing neighborhoods may be the group the campaign most needs to reach.

questions.prompt: Before the feature-positive call, a viral chart circles one rising blood marker but omits baseline range and repeat-test results. What should the fact-checker ask?
choices: Where are the baseline, repeat-test, and non-rising cases?
Which medical conditions does the rising marker indicate, since the rising marker's clinical meaning is the most useful context the chart could provide readers?
How was the chart's data collected, since methodology disclosure typically strengthens reader confidence in any single-marker visualization the chart presents?
questions.explanation: The missing baseline and repeat test can change the claim. The red circle is a feature, not the whole evidence base.

questions.prompt: Suppose feature-positive risk is present: a medical team sees no symptom in a patient, but the test is known to miss early cases. How should absent evidence be handled?
choices: Order the test again to confirm the absent symptom, since repeat testing addresses measurement noise more reliably than questioning the test's underlying sensitivity directly.
Document the absent symptom as a clear negative finding, since clear documentation supports the patient's chart accuracy across subsequent clinical decision points reliably.
Ask whether the absent symptom is reliable evidence or a limit of the test.
questions.explanation: Absence can matter, but only if the system would have detected the sign. The reliability of absence must be checked.

questions.prompt: Two feature-positive signals compete: a product manager wants to prevent visible user stories from crowding out silent users in roadmap meetings. Which practice helps most?
choices: Survey silent users directly through email outreach, since direct contact with silent users converts them into visible users the roadmap can incorporate fully.
Add an absent-evidence column beside every visible cue.
Require every user story to include silent-user implications, since cross-referencing visible and silent user types builds the awareness the team needs over time.
questions.explanation: The absent-evidence column forces the silent group into the decision without discarding visible stories.

reviewCards.front: A visible cue is driving the room. What missing evidence should balance the cue?
reviewCards.back: Ask which absent cues would change the judgment. Missing information needs a deliberate search, not silence.

reviewCards.front: What is the core correction?
reviewCards.back: Add an explicit absence check: what should be present, and who or what is missing?

reviewCards.front: When is absence meaningful?
reviewCards.back: When the system would reliably have detected the cue if it were there.

reviewCards.front: Why can no complaint mislead?
reviewCards.back: No complaint can mean no problem, no safe way to complain, or no one asked.

reviewCards.front: What should sit beside a visible story?
reviewCards.back: The silent group, missing records, baseline, or absent symptom that would change the choice.

chapters.title: Cherry-Picking
chapters.hook: A perfect set of facts can be dishonest when the missing cases are doing the work.
chapters.counterintuition: A true fact can still mislead when it was selected to hide the rest; name cherry-picking, then add the omitted cases before approving the claim.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Cherry-picking turns selected facts into a false whole. Correct it by asking what was left out before the decision moves.

breakdown.fastRead: The critic panel sees five airport screens where the new scoring rule found late departures. Gail is ready to approve the rule because every selected case looks damning. Then she points to the airport board and asks for the flights that left on time, the flights that arrived late for unrelated reasons, and the routes not shown at all. One accurate example may still come from a crooked sample. Cherry-picking is not a lie about one cherry. It is picking the cherries and hiding the tree.
breakdown.deepRead:
Cherry-picking works because selected facts can be real. The late flights really happened. The glowing testimonials really came from customers. The court examples really contain mistakes. That truth makes the trap harder to resist, because the argument does not feel fake. It feels supported.

The correction is to ask for the search rule. Who was included? Who was excluded? What cases would count against the claim? A claim backed by ten examples is weak if the speaker inspected a thousand cases and kept only the ten that helped. A claim backed by three failures may be strong if those were the only three cases in the file.

The missing cases are part of the evidence.

A medical-device review shows the move. Yvette hears a vendor present four hospitals with clean adverse-event logs. The stainless tasting spoon beside the lunch trays clinks while the room relaxes. Before signing the pilot, she asks whether any hospitals stopped using the device, failed to report, or logged events under another code. She is not calling the four clean logs false. She will not let omitted cases disappear.

That is the practical skill: use cherry-picking as the warning label, then make the specific correction before the choice moves forward. Request the denominator, the rejected cases, the time period, the search terms, and the evidence that would have embarrassed the claim. Selected facts can inform you only after the selection method is visible.
breakdown.fullRead:
The court file schedule is stacked on Janice's desk at 4:20 p.m. A lawyer wants the judge to see three borrowers who missed payments after refinancing. The loan worksheet looks decisive until Janice asks for the borrowers who refinanced and stayed current, the ones denied refinancing, and the dates used to build the file. The selected facts do not vanish. They shrink to their proper size.

Cherry-picking is often more dangerous than open invention because it borrows the dignity of evidence. A false number can be checked. A true number, carefully chosen, can walk through the door with a clean face. That is why the move has to happen before the room commits: mark the selection, ask what was not picked, and make the decision wait for the omitted cases.

Ask yourself one question: if this claim were wrong, which facts would its defender quietly leave in the basket?

A short history of medicine makes the pressure vivid. Taking the Medicine notes that the harm from smoking can be roughly as large as the combined benefit of postwar medical advances. If you display only new drugs, better surgery, and longer survival charts, modern medicine looks like a clean triumph. Add smoking's damage and the story changes. The cure is not cynicism about medicine. The cure is refusing to let selected facts pretend to be the whole field.

You can see the same shape in forecasting. Odette reviews a soccer playoff rule after a club director shows every year when the higher seed advanced. The shipping manifest from a delayed equipment order lies on the table, absurdly out of place, but it helps her slow down. She asks for seasons when the higher seed lost, years with changed injury rules, and games excluded because the format was different. The forecast becomes less dramatic and more useful.

Do not let selected facts pretend to be the whole field.

The Bible can be cherry-picked into almost any argument if verses are lifted without the surrounding passage. A wine harvest comparison has the same temptation in smaller form. Mireille can choose two sunny weeks, one flattering critic quote, and one scoreboard still from a tasting contest to call the vintage exceptional. Or she can include rain weeks, spoiled lots, low-scoring panels, and the comparison years that make the claim honest. The second version may sell less loudly, but it gives the buyer a real choice.

The limit is that complete evidence is rarely available. You cannot inspect every case before ordering lunch, hiring a contractor, or voting on a budget. The rule is not to demand perfect completeness. The rule is to notice when someone is asking a few vivid facts to stand in for a whole field. When the stakes are high, ask for the denominator. When the stakes are modest, ask for one contrary case. When the claim arrives polished, ask how the cherries were picked.

A true fact can still be a crooked sample. The honest move is to put the basket on the table.

examples.whatToDo: Ask for the flights omitted from the scoring sheet before accepting the pattern.
examples.whyItMatters: The late departures may be real, but they cannot represent the airline until the missing routes and clean departures are visible.

examples.whyItMatters: Three defaults can be important without proving the program failed. The missing borrowers decide what the examples mean.

examples.whyItMatters: Clean cases can be cherry-picked too. The safety claim needs the hospitals that make the product look worse.

questions.prompt: In a cherry-picking case, a charity report highlights five families helped by a grant, all photographed during the best week of the program, it says nothing about the applicants rejected, families who left early, or months when results fell. What is the cherry-picking risk?
choices: True stories are being used as if they represent the whole program without showing the omitted cases.
True stories are being told too briefly, since longer narratives typically capture the kind of program nuance summary photos cannot convey to donors at scale.
True stories are being collected during the wrong week, since week-of selection typically introduces seasonal bias unrelated to the program's underlying performance trend.
questions.explanation: The family stories may be true, but they were selected. The correction is to ask for rejected applicants, exits, weak months, and the denominator before judging the grant.

questions.prompt: During a cherry-picking review, a sales director shows six accounts that grew after a new pricing script, the slide omits accounts that received the script and shrank, plus accounts that grew before the script existed. What should you ask before approving the rollout?
choices: Ask which account managers handled the six growing accounts, since manager skill often explains account growth more than any pricing-script change does in practice.
Ask for exposed and unexposed accounts, plus the rule used to select the six examples.
Ask whether the script's pricing levels matched industry benchmarks, since industry-level comparisons validate the script's reasonableness across account types broadly.
questions.explanation: The right move exposes the selection method and omitted comparison groups. A slogan or inspiring story leaves the cherry-picking intact.

questions.prompt: When cherry-picking pressure appears, a candidate quotes three lines from a long policy hearing to prove that an opponent hates small businesses. The full transcript includes later support, exceptions, and a separate concern about tax fraud. Which response best corrects the error?
choices: Demand a public apology from the opponent for the original lines, since strong policy positions require public accountability regardless of context surrounding them.
Request a campaign-finance audit of the candidate, since candidates who selectively quote opponents often have other transparency problems worth investigating systematically.
Read the surrounding transcript and ask which lines were left out of the selection.
questions.explanation: The quotes can be accurate and still selected to distort meaning. The correction is context and omitted lines, not dueling cherry-picked fragments.

questions.prompt: After cherry-picking risk surfaces, a hospital vendor says its device is safe because three trial sites reported no incidents, one site withdrew, two sites changed reporting systems, and the vendor does not mention them. What is the strongest next decision?
choices: Pause approval until withdrawn and differently coded sites are included in the adverse-event review.
Approve the device with conditions, since three sites reporting no incidents is a strong enough signal to proceed with appropriate post-market monitoring overall.
Reject the device based on vendor opacity, since vendors that omit site-level details typically have additional issues that further investigation would surface.
questions.explanation: The clean sites matter only after the omitted sites are visible. Immediate approval accepts the selection; automatic rejection replaces analysis with suspicion.

questions.prompt: If cherry-picking reasoning takes over, a newsletter claims a forecasting model is brilliant by listing every year it called the winner correctly. It leaves out years it made no call, years it changed the call late, and years with changed rules. What makes this cherry-picking?
choices: The forecasting model uses inconsistent methodology across years, since rule changes between years invalidate any claim of consistent forecasting capability over time.
The newsletter has commercial incentive to promote the model, since promotional content typically overstates the model's accuracy across reporting cycles in financial markets.
The successes were chosen without the full set of attempts and misses.
questions.explanation: The selected wins are not enough. Forecasting evidence needs the full attempt record, including no-calls, late changes, misses, and altered conditions.

questions.prompt: While cherry-picking pressure builds, a manager wants to fire a contractor after collecting three angry emails, the folder also holds twenty quiet renewals and four satisfied clients who never wrote. Which action keeps selected facts from driving the choice?
choices: Investigate the three angry emails in detail, since direct investigation of complaints typically resolves the underlying issues before they affect other clients in the portfolio.
Compare angry emails with renewals, silent clients, and the total client count before deciding.
Survey all clients about their satisfaction levels, since systematic satisfaction data is more reliable than email-based feedback for major personnel decisions across teams.
questions.explanation: The angry emails may point to a problem, but the decision needs the omitted cases and denominator. Deleting them hides evidence in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Before the cherry-picking call, a nutrition influencer shows only blood-test panels from followers whose marker improved after buying a supplement. You are reviewing an ad claim before it goes live. Which question should block the claim until answered?
choices: Has the supplement been tested in a controlled trial, since controlled trials are the standard evidence framework for any health-related product claim under regulation?
How many followers tested, how many did not improve, and how were the displayed panels chosen?
Does the influencer disclose her commercial relationship with the supplement maker, since financial conflicts shape the credibility of any health claim made publicly?
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking hides in the selection rule. The ad needs the full test group and non-improvers, not better packaging around selected panels.

questions.prompt: Suppose cherry-picking risk is present: a school district promotes a reading program using only classrooms taught by its two most experienced teachers. It omits new teachers, classrooms that dropped the program, and schools with low attendance. What is the most precise diagnosis?
choices: The case set is too small to support program promotion, since two-teacher samples cannot represent the program's effectiveness across larger district populations confidently.
The case set should be expanded to include the most struggling classrooms, since struggling classroom outcomes signal where the program needs structural improvement next.
The case set was selected to flatter the program, so omitted classrooms must be added.
questions.explanation: The problem is not simply noise. The district chose favorable classrooms and left out cases that could weaken the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Two cherry-picking signals compete: a board packet uses three disaster stories to argue against expanding a ferry schedule. The packet excludes years when expanded schedules worked, weather differences, and maintenance periods. What is the cleanest correction?
choices: Build a table with all expanded-schedule years, conditions, failures, and successes before voting.
Build a separate packet specifically about the three disaster years, since detailed case studies of failures inform future expansion decisions more directly than aggregated tables.
Build a passenger-survey appendix for the packet, since passenger sentiment captures the kind of context the disaster stories alone cannot provide for the board.
questions.explanation: The correction is the full field of cases with conditions attached. Counter-cherry-picking with success stories would repeat the same error.

reviewCards.front: A claim is backed by vivid true examples. What omitted cases should be requested?
reviewCards.back: Request the failures, near misses, excluded cases, and denominator. True examples need the cases they left out.

reviewCards.front: Someone shows successes but not attempts. What is the missing check?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the denominator, the selection rule, and the failures that would weaken the claim.

reviewCards.front: A quote, chart, or testimonial feels decisive. What makes it honest?
reviewCards.back: It becomes useful only when the surrounding context and contrary cases are visible.

reviewCards.front: A forecast lists only its wins. What should you ask for?
reviewCards.back: Ask for misses, no-calls, changed calls, and excluded periods before trusting the pattern.

reviewCards.front: You cannot get the full dataset. What is the smaller correction?
reviewCards.back: Ask for one contrary case and one reason the displayed examples were selected.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Treat selected facts as a warning to ask for omitted cases before deciding.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a deck uses examples to prove a claim, then I will ask for the cases that would weaken it.
If a model lists wins, then I will ask for attempts, misses, no-calls, and changed calls.
If testimonials drive a purchase or policy, then I will ask how they were chosen and who was excluded.
If a quote feels decisive, then I will read the surrounding context before using it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one claim you heard today that uses examples. Write the selection rule you would need and one omitted case that could change your mind.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one persuasive chart or story by adding a denominator, contrary cases, and excluded periods.

chapters.tryThisNow: Take one claim backed by examples. Write the excluded cases you would expect to see if the claim were honest, then ask for them before deciding.

memorableLines.text: A true fact can still be a crooked sample.
The missing cases are part of the evidence.
Do not let selected facts pretend to be the whole field.

chapters.title: Fallacy of the Single Cause
chapters.hook: The neatest explanation is often the one that cut away the machinery.
chapters.counterintuition: A single cause feels useful because it is clean; map the interacting causes before the story starts choosing for you.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Single-cause stories make decisions feel clear while hiding the mechanism. Build a small cause map before assigning blame, credit, or action.

breakdown.fastRead: The triage desk blames a rise in patient dropouts on one rude intake clerk. Desmond can fire the clerk and feel decisive. Instead, he marks single cause on the dropout table and adds wait time, parking, referral wording, and evening staffing. The clerk may matter, but the mechanism is wider. A clean explanation can be a dirty map. The fallacy is not looking for causes. It is stopping at the first cause that makes the room feel finished.
breakdown.deepRead:
The fallacy of the single cause starts with a relief: now we know why it happened. One villain, one policy, one market shock, one bad hire, one clever feature. The explanation fits in a sentence, which makes it easy to repeat and easy to defend.

Real outcomes usually have joints. A seafood bid may fail because the cold-storage price rose, the export window moved, the buyer changed inspection rules, and the team assumed the old shipping rhythm still held. Any one factor can be true. None has to be the whole cause.

Single cause is comfort wearing a lab coat.

The correction is a mechanism map, not a lecture about complexity. Put the suspected cause in the center. Add two enabling conditions, one missing restraint, and one alternative path that could produce the same result. Then ask which lever the next decision can actually move. Multi-causality is useful only when it changes the choice in front of you.

A fintech review shows the difference. Evelyn sees a default model fail and hears the room blame one new variable. The maintenance key on the table belongs to the office server rack, and she uses it as a prop: one key does not open every lock. Before approving the rollback, she maps stale income data, a changed fraud rule, a vendor delay, and borrower seasonality. The rollback becomes narrower, faster, and less theatrical.
breakdown.fullRead:
The port scheduling office smells of wet rope and old printer toner. Bethany watches a storm track crawl across the screen while a dispatcher says the missed sailings were caused by one cautious supervisor. The claim is tempting because it gives the port a person to correct. Bethany writes Tolstoy in the margin, then draws arrows from wind timing, tug availability, crew-hour limits, and the new customs inspection window. The next choice changes: she revises the schedule rule instead of disciplining one supervisor.

The fallacy of the single cause does not mean one cause is never important. Sometimes one fuse really did blow. Sometimes one contract clause, one wrong dose, or one broken pipe deserves urgent attention. The error is treating a clean explanation as proof that the other parts of the mechanism can be ignored.

What else had to be true for this cause to matter?

War and Peace keeps returning to the same pressure: great events do not move because one person pulls one lever. Tolstoy's battle scenes make single-cause history look too tidy for human systems. Commanders give orders, soldiers misunderstand, mud slows movement, fear changes timing, and later a story turns the mess into one clean cause. Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons use that kind of intuition failure to show how easily a vivid explanation can crowd out the unseen network behind it.

A school literacy case has the same shape in smaller form. Moira sees a reading intervention miss its target, and the clean explanation is that parents did not practice at home. The booking ledger shows another pattern: substitute teachers, late bus arrivals, testing-week interruptions, and a change in library hours all hit the same group. Parent practice still belongs on the map. It no longer gets to carry the whole failure alone.

The mechanism map should change the next choice, not decorate the old one.

The limited bakery batch gives a softer example. Glenn's almond loaves sell out by 10:30 a.m., and the grant rubric for a small-business award praises scarcity as the cause. In the postmortem, he adds rain that pushed commuters indoors, a nearby conference break, a social post from a local critic, and a smaller batch size after a flour delivery problem. Scarcity helped. It was not the engine by itself. The next batch plan changes because the cause map changed.

The practical test is simple. If your explanation names one cause, ask whether it is a trigger, an enabling condition, a background pressure, or a story-friendly symbol. A trigger starts motion. An enabling condition lets it matter. A background pressure raises the odds. A symbol makes people nod. Confusing these roles creates bad action: firing a person when a process failed, copying a tactic when timing did the work, or blaming culture when incentives and constraints made the behavior rational.

The limit is that maps can become fog. You do not need twenty arrows before deciding. You need enough causes to stop the first neat story from pretending to be the mechanism. For a small choice, add two other causes. For a high-stakes choice, add the sequence: trigger, conditions, constraints, and feedback loop. Then decide from the map you can defend.

examples.scenario: The dropout table sits under a triage monitor in a Halifax emergency desk at 8:40 p.m. Desmond, the shift lead, must decide whether one rude clerk caused the lost patients. examples.whyItMatters: The clerk may matter, but firing one person will miss the mechanism if waits, wording, and staffing made the dropouts likely.

examples.whyItMatters: A higher storage quote can be real without being the only cause. The next bid needs the whole chain.

examples.whyItMatters: A full rollback may satisfy the room, but it can damage a working model if several causes created the spike.

examples.whyItMatters: Parent practice may matter, but the intervention fails differently if transport, staffing, and access are also causes.

examples.title: Glenn rewrites the batch postmortem
examples.scenario: Why did the almond loaves vanish before the lunch rush when last week's batch sat untouched? Glenn reviews the Manchester bakery postmortem at 11:05 a.m. with a grant rubric beside the register. He marks fallacy, adds rain, a conference break, and batch size, then changes the next bake plan.
examples.whatToDo: Explain the sellout with several causes before scaling the batch.
examples.whyItMatters: Scarcity may help sales, but copying it alone ignores traffic, weather, publicity, and production limits.

questions.prompt: In a fallacy-single case, a hospital team says patient complaints rose because one new receptionist has a sharp tone, the same month added a new intake form, longer parking walks, and fewer evening nurses. What is the fallacy of the single cause?
choices: Treating the receptionist as the whole explanation before mapping the other causes.
Failing to verify the receptionist's actual behavior with patient interviews, since direct patient testimony reveals which interactions actually drove complaint rates.
Allowing one employee's interpersonal style to overshadow the team's broader operational performance during the same review period for the patient experience.
questions.explanation: The receptionist may matter, but the error is letting one cause absorb the form, parking, and staffing changes.

questions.prompt: During a fallacy-single review, a seafood exporter loses a bid and blames the cold-storage quote, the buyer also shortened the inspection window, changed credit terms, and ordered less volume. What should the manager do before switching vendors?
choices: Renegotiate the cold-storage quote, since the visible cost factor is the lever the exporter can actually move while other factors remain outside its control.
Reject the bid loss as final and move on to the next customer, since post-mortem analysis of a lost bid often produces no actionable lessons for future bids.
Map storage cost, inspection timing, credit terms, and order volume before choosing a lever.
questions.explanation: The storage quote is only one piece. A cause map points to the lever that actually changes the next bid.

questions.prompt: When fallacy-single pressure appears, a port director says one cautious supervisor caused three missed sailings. Logs show wind timing, tug shortages, customs delays, and crew-hour limits. Which action best breaks the single-cause story?
choices: Build a sequence showing how the supervisor's call interacted with weather, tugs, customs, and crew limits.
Discipline the supervisor for the missed sailings, since accountability for operational decisions is what drives port culture and reliability over the long term.
Replace the cautious supervisor with a more aggressive scheduler, since the port needs leadership willing to operate under marginal conditions during weather pressure.
questions.explanation: The best answer keeps the supervisor in the picture but adds the conditions that made the call produce missed sailings.

questions.prompt: After fallacy-single risk surfaces, a model review blames a default spike on one new variable, the spike also follows stale income data, a changed fraud rule, and a vendor delay. What is the most useful next move?
choices: Revert the new variable in the next release, since the visible correlation between the variable's introduction and the spike justifies cautious rollback before debate.
Draw a mechanism map and test which cause or interaction the next release can change.
Re-train the model from scratch with cleaner data, since model issues that span multiple causes often resolve through complete retraining more reliably than targeted fixes.
questions.explanation: A mechanism map avoids both overreaction and paralysis. It finds which part of the causal chain the next release can move.

questions.prompt: If fallacy-single reasoning takes over, a school blames weak reading scores on parents not practicing at home. Calendar notes show substitute coverage, bus delays, library closures, and testing-week disruptions. Which conclusion is strongest?
choices: Parent practice may be one cause, but the intervention plan should include the timing and access constraints.
Parent practice is the underlying root cause, since literacy outcomes are predominantly driven by home reading time across most school populations consistently.
Parent practice is the wrong frame for school analysis, since school-day variables fall within the school's actual operational control and should drive interventions.
questions.explanation: The parent-practice story becomes usable only after the other causes are added to the plan.

questions.prompt: While fallacy-single pressure builds, a bakery owner says scarcity alone made a small batch sell out, the sellout happened during heavy rain, a nearby conference break, and a local critic's post. What should he do before doubling down on scarcity?
choices: Double the batch size for next weekend, since the sellout demonstrates the bakery's underlying demand capacity is larger than current production assumes broadly.
Reduce the batch size further to maintain scarcity, since scarcity-driven demand is the lever the owner has most directly under his daily operational control.
Compare batch size with traffic, weather, publicity, and timing before changing production.
questions.explanation: Scarcity may help, but the next bake plan needs the interacting causes that created the sellout.

questions.prompt: Before the fallacy-single call, a nonprofit director says donations fell because the newsletter subject line was dull. The same week, a payment link broke for mobile users and a matching grant expired. What question best tests the explanation?
choices: Why did the subject line miss the team's review process, since editorial review failures are the most common cause of underperforming newsletter campaigns generally?
Did the matching grant expiration reduce donor enthusiasm, since matching grants drive significant short-term gift volume across nonprofit campaigns reliably?
Which causes changed at the same time, and which one can the next campaign isolate or repair?
questions.explanation: The useful question maps simultaneous causes and turns them into testable levers. A better subject line alone may miss the broken link.

questions.prompt: Turnover rises after remote work expands, and a retention lead blames damaged culture. Payroll records show a pay freeze, a new competitor hiring nearby, and a promotion backlog. What is wrong with the clean story?
choices: It treats culture as the single cause while ignoring incentives, labor market pressure, and career paths.
It treats culture as a measurable variable, when culture is actually too diffuse to evaluate using the kind of metrics retention reviews typically rely on.
It treats remote work as the only relevant change, when remote work is itself just one of several workplace shifts the company has been navigating recently.
questions.explanation: Remote work or culture may still matter, but the clean story hides other causes that affect turnover directly.

questions.prompt: Two fallacy-single signals compete: a city task force explains a crash increase by blaming one confusing sign. The same intersection had a new delivery zone, changed light timing, and more cyclists after a bridge closure. Which plan best handles the causal claim?
choices: Replace the confusing sign immediately, since sign design is the variable the city can fix at lowest cost and visible action builds community trust effectively.
Map sign design, delivery blockage, light timing, and cyclist volume before choosing the first intervention.
Restrict cyclist access until the bridge reopens, since cyclist volume is the single most prominent change the intersection has absorbed during the closure period.
questions.explanation: The sign may be a cause, but the task force should choose from the mapped mechanism, not from the neatest object to blame.

reviewCards.front: A room has one clean explanation for a messy result. What additional causes must be mapped?
reviewCards.back: Map multiple contributing causes and their links. One clean factor may be real while still being incomplete.

reviewCards.front: A cause feels obvious. What should go on the small map?
reviewCards.back: Add the suspected cause, two enabling conditions, one missing restraint, and one alternative path.

reviewCards.front: A person is being blamed for an outcome. What should you check?
reviewCards.back: Check which system conditions made that person's action matter before assigning the whole cause.

reviewCards.front: A tactic worked once and everyone names one reason. What is the risk?
reviewCards.back: The named reason may be only a trigger while timing, constraints, or background pressure did the work.

reviewCards.front: Your map has become too complex. What is enough for a live decision?
reviewCards.back: Add just enough causes to stop the first neat story from pretending to be the whole mechanism.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Replace one-cause stories with a small mechanism map before assigning blame, credit, or action.

ifThenPlans.plan: If one person is named as the cause, then I will list the conditions that made that action matter.
If one tactic gets all the credit, then I will add timing, constraints, and background pressure.
If a failure has a neat explanation, then I will map trigger, enabling condition, restraint, and feedback.
If a proposed fix targets one cause, then I will ask which other causes remain after the fix.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one explanation you heard today. Write the named cause, two enabling conditions, and one alternative path before repeating it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, turn one blame or credit story into a four-part mechanism map before deciding what to change.

chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one neat explanation you recently accepted. Add two enabling conditions and one alternative cause before you repeat it.

memorableLines.text: A clean explanation can be a dirty map.
Single cause is comfort wearing a lab coat.
The mechanism map should change the next choice, not decorate the old one.

chapters.title: Intention-to-Treat Error
chapters.hook: The people who leave the trial may be the people telling you whether it worked.
chapters.counterintuition: A cleaner success rate can be less honest; keep people in their assigned groups before the dropouts make the result look better than it is.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Intention-to-treat protects the original comparison. Count people by assigned group, including switchers and dropouts, before deciding what worked.

breakdown.fastRead: The wildfire planning room celebrates a fuel-saving route because the crews that finished the test used less fuel. Carolyn points to the fuel receipt pile and asks about crews assigned to the route who abandoned it during smoke, detours, or equipment trouble. The result changes. Intention-to-treat error appears when you judge only the people who stuck with the plan. The people who leave the trial may be the people telling you whether it worked.
breakdown.deepRead:
A clean result often comes from cleaning away the difficult people. The patients who stopped taking the drug, the users who left the beta, the crews who abandoned the route, the investors who moved their money, and the students who missed sessions all make the table untidy. Removing them can make the treatment, feature, route, fund, or program look stronger.

Intention-to-treat keeps the comparison honest by counting people in the groups they were assigned to at the start. If a clinical trial assigns one group to a treatment and another to a control, the result should not quietly erase the people who quit because of side effects, confusion, cost, or lack of benefit. Those exits are not administrative noise. They are part of what the treatment does in the world.

Dropouts are evidence with their coats on.

The correction is to protect the assignment before reading the outcome. Ask who was assigned, who switched, who dropped out, and whether the headline result counts all of them. Then decide from the assigned groups, not from the tidiest survivors.

A software beta shows the move. Jeffrey sees a dashboard where active users love the prototype. Before green-lighting the feature, he marks assigned groups on the prototype log and adds the users who were invited but never activated, the users who quit after two sessions, and the users who switched back to the old flow. He is not punishing the feature. He is keeping the comparison from being edited by endurance.
breakdown.fullRead:
The biotech signal review starts with a flattering chart. Lillian sees a control chart where the patients who completed all visits improved more than the control group. The room wants to call the signal promising. Then she asks for the assigned groups: everyone offered the treatment, everyone assigned to control, the patients who dropped because of nausea, the patients who missed visits, and the ones who crossed over to another therapy.

The intention-to-treat principle exists because compliance is not neutral. People do not drop out at random. They quit because the treatment hurts, disappoints, costs too much, confuses them, or fails to fit their life. If you count only the finishers, you may be measuring the treatment plus the special qualities of people able to finish it. The assigned group is the anchor that keeps the comparison from drifting.

Who disappeared from the success rate?

Statistical Considerations in the Intent-to-Treat Principle, associated with Lachin's work on clinical trials, puts pressure on this exact point: the analysis should preserve the randomized or assigned comparison as far as possible. That is not a technical courtesy. It is a guardrail against letting the result be rewritten after the hard cases leave.

A cycling crash audit makes the error visible outside medicine. You are looking at an exam sheet for riders assigned to a safety course. Regina, the city analyst, must decide whether the course reduced crashes. The simple report counts only riders who completed every session. She adds riders assigned to the course who skipped sessions after near misses, riders who changed routes, and riders who stopped cycling. The crash rate becomes less flattering and more useful.

The assigned group is the promise the evidence made before it knew the answer.

A touring theater budget shows the same pattern. Murray reviews a market memo saying the new subscription plan improved attendance among subscribers who stayed all season. The missing people are the ones assigned to the offer who canceled after the first show, failed to redeem tickets, or moved to single purchases. If the budget counts only loyal subscribers, the plan looks like magic. If it counts the assigned group, the plan looks like a tool with friction.

The practical correction is a small table. Column one: assigned to the option. Column two: completed as planned. Column three: switched or quit. Column four: outcome counted where? If the report jumps from assigned people to finishers without explaining the missing column, you are looking at a possible intention-to-treat error.

The limit is that no analysis can make missing data perfect. Some people vanish completely. Some switch for reasons nobody recorded. Some outcomes cannot be recovered. Still, the first honest question remains stable: what happened to everyone who was originally assigned? When the answer is unclear, lower your confidence. When the answer is visible, let the assigned groups carry the decision.

examples.whatToDo: Count crews by original route assignment before judging fuel savings.
examples.whyItMatters: The finishers may have saved fuel because the difficult cases left the test. The abandoned assignments belong in the result.

examples.whyItMatters: The feature may look strong because the frustrated or confused users disappeared before the chart was drawn.

examples.title: Cecile reopens the pension postmortem

Cecile reviews the Montreal pension committee postmortem at 4:05 p.m. with a closed-door list beside the binders. She marks intention, adds members assigned to advice who opted out or changed funds, and changes the performance note.
examples.whatToDo: Track the advice program from assignment through opt-outs before judging performance.
examples.whyItMatters: The remaining participants may be unusually engaged. The people who left are part of the program's real effect.

planSpec.domain: a pension fund committee applying Intention-to-Treat Error under operational pressure

questions.prompt: In a intention-treat case, a clinical trial report says patients who completed a therapy improved more than controls, it excludes patients assigned to the therapy who quit because of nausea or missed visits. What is the intention-to-treat risk?
choices: The report judges only finishers and drops people whose assignment may reveal the therapy's real cost.
The report selects an analytical method that handles missing data through imputation, which most clinical reviewers recognize as defensible across therapy contexts broadly.
The report omits the control group's dropout rate, which is itself a problem for the comparison but separate from intention-to-treat analysis specifically.
questions.explanation: The error is not that improvement is fake. The error is removing assigned patients whose dropout may be part of the treatment effect.

questions.prompt: During a intention-treat review, a software beta shows strong satisfaction among active users, the company invited 4,000 people, but only 900 activated and many quit after two sessions. What should the launch review compare?
choices: Only the 900 active users' satisfaction, since active users represent the population the company should optimize for in subsequent product development cycles broadly.
The invited beta group, activations, early quits, and outcomes against the assigned comparison group.
Active users' satisfaction plus a comparison with competitor product satisfaction, since competitive context shapes how to interpret any internal satisfaction score in beta.
questions.explanation: The assigned group protects the comparison. Active users matter, but so do non-activations and early quits.

questions.prompt: When intention-treat pressure appears, a safety course claims riders who completed all sessions had fewer crashes. The audit omits riders assigned to the course who stopped cycling after early near misses. Which correction fits intention-to-treat?
choices: Analyze all assigned riders in the course group, including non-completers and riders who stopped cycling.
Analyze only riders who completed every course session, since complete-protocol review captures the real impact on participants who were properly exposed to it.
Analyze riders who completed at least half the sessions, since partial completion is enough exposure to count as meaningful course participation for crash-rate analysis.
questions.explanation: The assigned riders who stopped cycling may hold the safety cost. Finisher-only analysis can flatter the course.

questions.prompt: After intention-treat risk surfaces, a theater subscription looks profitable among patrons who stayed all season, the budget excludes patrons assigned to the offer who canceled after one show or never redeemed tickets. What is wrong with the budget claim?
choices: It overstates profitability by including the subscription discount when the budget should reflect full-price revenue from comparable single-show purchases instead.
It changes the comparison after outcomes are known by removing assigned patrons who left.
It fails to account for canceled patrons' negative word-of-mouth, which damages future subscription revenue beyond the immediate canceled-patron line item itself.
questions.explanation: The budget edits the assigned group after seeing behavior. Cancellations and non-redemptions belong in the plan's effect.

questions.prompt: If intention-treat reasoning takes over, a wildfire route test reports fuel savings among crews that finished the assigned route. Several crews abandoned the route due to smoke, detours, or equipment trouble. What decision is most defensible?
choices: Review fuel use by original route assignment, including crews that abandoned the route and why.
Review fuel use only for crews that completed the assigned route, since completion verifies the route was actually tested under operational conditions appropriate for the data.
Review smoke exposure data for abandoning crews, since environmental context explains the abandonment pattern and informs whether the route is viable in future seasons.
questions.explanation: The abandonment is part of the route's real performance. Counting only finishers may hide the conditions where the route fails.

questions.prompt: While intention-treat pressure builds, a pension advice program reports better returns among members who attended all sessions, it omits members assigned to advice who opted out, moved funds, or stopped replying. What should the committee request?
choices: A detailed analysis of attending members' demographics, since demographic context explains the return patterns within the attending segment more directly than aggregate analysis.
A comparison of returns between attending members and the general fund average, since benchmarking against the average validates the program's effect on persistent attendees.
A table from assignment to attendance, opt-outs, fund moves, and returns for every assigned member.
questions.explanation: The committee needs the assignment-to-outcome path. Committed attendees may not represent the program's effect on everyone assigned.

questions.prompt: Before the intention-treat call, a training vendor says its leadership course works because managers who completed every module were promoted faster. The client list excludes assigned managers who dropped out after workload conflicts. Which question matters most?
choices: What promotion criteria the company applies, since promotion criteria shape whether completing the course actually correlates with the outcomes the vendor claims.
What other leadership development resources the promoted managers used, since multi-channel development typically combines into the promotion outcomes the vendor reports.
What happened to every manager originally assigned to the course, including dropouts?
questions.explanation: Promotions among completers may reflect who could finish. Intention-to-treat asks about the whole assigned group.

questions.prompt: Suppose intention-treat risk is present: a diet app claims users who logged meals for eight weeks lost weight. It excludes people assigned to the app who stopped logging after week one. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The app may be measuring persistent loggers instead of the effect of assigning people to the app.
Persistent loggers likely lost weight before they joined the program, since pre-existing motivation often correlates with both app usage and weight loss patterns.
The result probably reflects users with stronger life-circumstance support, since support networks predict weight loss success more reliably than any specific app's features.
questions.explanation: The finisher group may differ from the assigned group. The omitted early stopouts can change the apparent effect.

questions.prompt: Two intention-treat signals compete: a tutoring program reports gains among students who attended ten sessions. The district assigned 300 students, but 110 missed at least half the sessions after schedule conflicts. Which plan protects the comparison?
choices: Analyze only the 190 students who attended ten sessions, since complete-attendance review captures the program's measured impact on those who took the full dose.
Analyze all assigned students by original assignment, with attendance and missing sessions shown.
Analyze the 110 students who missed sessions to identify schedule-conflict patterns, since conflict patterns inform future scheduling more directly than aggregate program analysis.
questions.explanation: The comparison starts at assignment. Attendance still matters, but it should be shown instead of used to erase students.

reviewCards.front: A success rate counts only people who finished. Who must stay in the denominator?
reviewCards.back: Keep dropouts, switchers, and noncompliers in the assigned groups. Completion-only rates can flatter the intervention.

reviewCards.front: A trial result looks cleaner after dropouts disappear. What is the danger?
reviewCards.back: The missing people may be the evidence that the treatment was hard, harmful, confusing, or weak.

reviewCards.front: A beta dashboard shows active users love the feature. What comparison is missing?
reviewCards.back: Compare everyone assigned or invited to the beta, including people who never activated or quit early.

reviewCards.front: A program counts only loyal participants. What table should you ask for?
reviewCards.back: Ask for assigned, completed, switched or quit, and where each outcome was counted.

reviewCards.front: Some assigned people vanished completely. What should happen to confidence?
reviewCards.back: Lower confidence and make the missing assigned group visible instead of treating finishers as the whole effect.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Protect the original assigned groups before judging whether an option worked.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a result reports finishers, then I will ask for everyone originally assigned.
If active users look happy, then I will ask who was invited, who never activated, and who quit.
If completers improve, then I will compare assigned students or employees including missed sessions.
If loyal participants outperform, then I will include opt-outs, switchers, and silent members.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one result based on completers. Write the original assigned group, the dropouts, and where the missing outcomes were counted.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit one program metric by drawing the path from assignment to completion, switch, dropout, and outcome.

chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one result that counts finishers. Write the original assigned group, then add the dropouts before trusting the success rate.

memorableLines.text: Dropouts are evidence with their coats on.
The assigned group is the promise the evidence made before it knew the answer.
The people who leave the trial may be the people telling you whether it worked.

chapters.title: News Illusion
chapters.hook: The alert feels like a handle on the world; often it is only a handle on your attention.
chapters.counterintuition: Being updated can leave you less prepared when novelty crowds out actionability, base rates, and slower evidence.
chapters.keyTakeaway: News illusion makes fresh information feel useful because it is fresh. Test whether it changes a decision, a model, or a measurable reality.

breakdown.fastRead: The coffee deal shifts after a headline about frost in Brazil. Jacqueline is ready to reopen the price before the ship window closes. Then she marks news illusion on a postmortem note and asks what the alert changes: stock, contract terms, crop data, or ship risk. The answer is almost nothing today. Novelty is not the same as signal. The next move is not to ignore the world. It is to stop an alert from acting like useful proof.
breakdown.deepRead:
News illusion starts with motion. A headline arrives, a chart flashes, a reporter sounds urgent, and your mind treats the update as if it has moved you closer to reality. Sometimes it has. Often it has only moved your attention.

The test is actionability. What decision changes because of this item? What number in your model changes? What base rate did it update? What slower source would confirm or correct it? If the answer is vague, the item may be interesting without being useful.

If the news cannot change a decision, it has only rented your attention.

A neonatal checklist review shows the difference. Patrice hears a clip about a rare equipment failure in another country and wants to rewrite the checklist before the night shift. The commitment card beside the incubator forces a pause. She asks whether the failure matches their equipment, whether the rate changed, and whether the existing checklist would catch it. The alert becomes a watch item, not a rewrite.

The correction is visible: place the fresh item beside the reality check. Put novelty in one column and actionability in the next. If the item changes a decision, name the decision. If it changes a number, write the old and new number. If it changes nothing, do not let it spend the day as if it did.
breakdown.fullRead:
The winter shelter allocation meeting begins with a video clip from a city two provinces away. Rhonda watches a reporter stand beside a crowded entrance and say shelters are overwhelmed. The room feels the pressure immediately. Then she touches the open-loop list taped to the wall and asks for local bed counts, weather forecasts, staff absences, and the number of people turned away last week. The video remains serious. It does not get to allocate tonight's vans by itself.

News illusion is not the claim that current events never matter. A bridge closure, a product recall, a court ruling, a storm warning, or a bank failure can change reality fast. The error is treating novelty as if it automatically brings usefulness. Freshness is a property of the item, not proof that the item belongs in your decision.

What would you do differently after reading it?

A goalkeeper academy gives the trap a physical form. You are looking at a news alert queue while Ursula, the academy director, must decide whether to replace a drill after a viral clip shows a keeper mishandling a high cross. She writes attention diet on the queue, checks their own save data, asks whether the clip matches the age group, and keeps the drill while adding one targeted variation. The clip becomes a prompt for checking reality, not a remote control.

A calmer source can tell you more by arriving less often.

The flood insurance desk shows the same discipline. Alfred sees three articles about dramatic flooding and wants to call every client in the low-risk tier. The clipboard has claims by postal code, elevation, policy gaps, and drainage projects. Once those are checked, the calls change: high-exposure clients get a clear review; low-exposure clients get a scheduled annual note. The news supplied urgency. The records supplied direction.

A newsroom meeting can fall for the same illusion it sells. Rosemary reviews a sealed envelope holding reader complaints after a front-page story drove clicks but produced no practical follow-up. In the postmortem, she marks news on the envelope and separates novelty, public consequence, reader action, and verification strength. The next front-page meeting changes because a story no longer wins only by being fresh. It must also tell readers what reality has changed.

The practical rule is an attention diet, not an information fast. Keep sources that improve your models, reveal risks you can act on, or give periodic summaries with context. Cut sources that create urgency without decisions. Delay sources that are useful only after several updates accumulate. In a workday, that may mean checking supply risk once after inventory, reading a weekly policy brief instead of twenty alerts, or saving a breaking story until you know what choice it could affect.

The limit is timing. Waiting for perfect context can be dangerous when a real emergency is unfolding. The answer is not slowness for its own sake. The answer is to ask whether the item is a warning, a decision input, or a distraction dressed as relevance. Warnings can interrupt. Decision inputs earn a place in the model. Distractions do not get to call themselves awareness.

examples.scenario: The postmortem note lies beside green coffee samples in a Hamburg supplier office at 7:25 a.m. Jacqueline, the buyer, must decide whether a frost headline should reopen the price. examples.whatToDo: Ask what the fresh alert changes in the actual negotiation before moving price.
examples.whyItMatters: A headline can be true without changing today's stock, contract, or delivery risk.

examples.whyItMatters: The articles create urgency, but the records show who actually needs a call.

examples.scenario: What did yesterday's front page help readers do after the clicks faded? Rosemary reviews the newsroom postmortem in Dublin at 5:35 p.m. with a sealed envelope of complaints on the table. She marks news, separates novelty from public consequence, and changes the next front-page test.
examples.whatToDo: Ask whether the story changed reality or only captured attention.
examples.whyItMatters: A story can be fresh and still leave readers no better prepared. The postmortem needs consequence, not only clicks.

planSpec.domain: a newsroom front-page meeting applying News Illusion under operational pressure

questions.prompt: In a news-illusion case, a procurement lead sees a breaking headline about a crop disease and wants to reopen a supplier price immediately, inventory, contract windows, and delivery dates have not changed. What is the news illusion risk?
choices: The alert feels useful because it is fresh, even though it has not changed the decision inputs.
The alert may be a leading indicator the procurement lead should respond to before the underlying contract data catches up to the reality on the ground.
The procurement lead may be using the alert to justify a pricing renegotiation she had wanted for unrelated reasons before the headline appeared in the news.
questions.explanation: The headline may be true, but actionability is missing. The buyer needs a changed input, not just a fresh item.

questions.prompt: During a news-illusion review, a hospital team hears about a rare equipment failure overseas and wants to rewrite a neonatal checklist before the night shift, the part number and local incident rate are still unknown. What should happen first?
choices: Rewrite the checklist immediately to address the overseas failure pattern, since checklist updates are cheap and the precaution principle favors quick action.
Check whether the alert applies locally and whether it changes a specific action tonight.
Notify all night-shift staff about the overseas failure, since informed staff make better decisions even when the failure pattern has not been verified locally.
questions.explanation: The alert earns attention, but it must pass through local equipment and actionability before changing the checklist.

questions.prompt: When news-illusion pressure appears, a shelter coordinator sees a viral clip of overcrowding in another city. Local bed counts, weather, and turnaway numbers do not yet show the same pressure. Which move best tests the appearance created by the clip?
choices: Expand shelter capacity preemptively after seeing the spread of that footage, since other cities' overcrowding signals a pattern the coordinator should address before it arrives.
Ignore the clip altogether, since out-of-city media coverage rarely reflects the operational conditions any single shelter is actually facing on the ground.
Compare the clip with local beds, weather, staffing, and recent turnaways.
questions.explanation: The clip may point to a real issue, but the allocation should follow local signal instead of novelty alone.

questions.prompt: After news-illusion risk surfaces, a coach wants to replace a training drill after a viral clip shows one professional making a costly mistake, her own players' data does not show the same weakness. What is the best decision?
choices: Keep the drill unchanged or add a targeted variation only if local player data supports it.
Replace the drill with a new one based on the viral clip, since visible high-level mistakes signal weaknesses worth addressing in any training program preventively.
Add the drill to other training programs in the same league, since visible professional mistakes generally translate into widespread training adjustments across teams broadly.
questions.explanation: The clip becomes useful only if it updates the academy's own model. Otherwise it is attention, not instruction.

questions.prompt: If news-illusion reasoning takes over, an insurance adviser reads three dramatic flood stories and wants to call every low-risk client. Claims by postal code and elevation show exposure is concentrated elsewhere. What should guide the calls?
choices: Calls to every low-risk client based on the flood stories, since visible recent events warrant proactive client outreach regardless of the underlying exposure profile.
A claims and exposure check that turns the fresh stories into targeted client action.
A coordinated email campaign across all postal codes, since email outreach is more efficient than calls and reaches the broader client base during news-driven moments.
questions.explanation: The stories supply urgency, but the claims and exposure records decide who needs action.

questions.prompt: While news-illusion pressure builds, a newsroom celebrates a story because it generated clicks all morning, in the postmortem, nobody can say what changed for readers or what action the story enabled. What is the strongest critique?
choices: The story's writers did not coordinate with the editorial board, since editorial alignment is essential for stories that generate the kind of attention the morning clicks signal.
The story's headline was too clickbait-y, since attention-driven headlines typically fail the kind of consequence test the newsroom should be applying to its work.
Novelty and attention were counted, but consequence and usefulness were not tested.
questions.explanation: The issue is not that clicks are meaningless. The postmortem needs consequence, verification strength, and reader action.

questions.prompt: Before the news-illusion call, a manager checks headlines between every task and says it keeps her aware. Her decisions rarely change, and she misses slower weekly reports that would update her forecasts. Which replacement fits the skill?
choices: Increase the frequency of headline checks, since more frequent monitoring catches the kind of news that affects decisions more reliably than scheduled checks would.
Subscribe to additional news sources, since broader news coverage reduces the chance of missing the kind of signal that actually changes a manager's forecast decisions.
Move alerts into scheduled checks and protect slower sources that change forecasts.
questions.explanation: The point is an attention diet, not ignorance. Scheduled checks and slower sources preserve information that changes decisions.

questions.prompt: Suppose news-illusion risk is present: a policy analyst reads twenty updates about a court case but cannot name one model, risk, or recommendation that changed. A weekly legal brief would summarize the same case with context. What is the better approach?
choices: Use the weekly brief unless a specific alert changes a decision before then.
Cancel the news subscriptions outright, since news consumption that produces no decision changes wastes the analyst's time on information that fails to inform any model.
Subscribe to additional court-case alert services, since broader alert coverage increases the chance of catching the specific information that changes the recommendation.
questions.explanation: The weekly brief may carry more signal because it arrives with context. Alerts earn interruption only when they change a live choice.

questions.prompt: Two news-illusion signals compete: a supply team watches live shipping alerts all day. Most alerts do not affect inventory or customer promises, while a daily carrier report changes decisions. Which rule would reduce news illusion?
choices: Let only alerts that change inventory, promises, or risk interrupt the day.
Schedule all shipping alerts into a single daily review window, since batched processing handles alert volume more efficiently than continuous interruption typically does.
Replace the live alerts with a real-time dashboard, since visual dashboards convey alert information more efficiently than text-based notifications during operational decisions.
questions.explanation: The interruption should be earned by actionability. If the daily report changes decisions, it has more signal than constant novelty.

reviewCards.front: A fresh alert feels important. What actionability test should filter it?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the alert changes a decision, forecast, or risk control. Freshness alone is not signal.

reviewCards.front: A headline makes you want to act. What is the first check?
reviewCards.back: Ask what decision, number, model, or risk estimate changed because of the item.

reviewCards.front: A vivid story from elsewhere creates pressure. What should you compare it with?
reviewCards.back: Compare it with local reality: counts, exposure, constraints, and the slower evidence that guides action.

reviewCards.front: Your feed keeps you aware but not better prepared. What adjustment helps?
reviewCards.back: Move novelty into scheduled checks and protect sources that update decisions with context.

reviewCards.front: A real emergency is unfolding. Does the attention diet still apply?
reviewCards.back: Yes: treat it as a warning only if it changes a decision, risk, or action now.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Test fresh information for actionability before letting it steer attention or decisions.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an alert arrives, then I will ask what decision or number it changes before interrupting work.
If a vivid outside story creates pressure, then I will compare it with local counts and constraints.
If a source creates urgency without action, then I will move it to a scheduled check or cut it.
If a story gets attention, then I will ask what consequence, action, or reality changed.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For one day, write one sentence beside each major alert: the decision it changes, or no decision.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, replace one high-frequency source with a slower source that updates a real model or decision.

chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one alert from today. Write the decision, number, or risk it changes; if none changes, close it without follow-up.

memorableLines.text: Novelty is not the same as signal.
If the news cannot change a decision, it has only rented your attention.
A calmer source can tell you more by arriving less often.
